title: Family, articles and possessives
objectives: I can name my family members and say who is who in a photo.
I can use definite and indefinite articles with the correct gender and number.
I can form regular plurals, including nouns that end in -ão, -l and -m.
I can say that something belongs to me, to you or to someone else.
I can talk about my pets and say whether I am single or married.

vocabulary.note: The plural of o pai also means parents. Do not confuse it with os países, the countries.
Brazilians say mãe directly to their mothers and mamãe is also common for children.
The plural os irmãos means brothers, or brothers and sisters.
The plural os filhos means sons, or children in general.
Often shortened to vô in speech.
Often shortened to vó in speech.
The plural os tios means uncles, or uncles and aunts.
Brazilian children also call family friends and teachers tio and tia as a sign of affection.

example.pt: O primo da Ana é alto.

vocabulary.note: The everyday word is often a mulher, which means both the woman and the wife.
The plural os sobrinhos means nephews, or nephews and nieces.

example.en: My nephew is five years old.
My niece is ten years old.

dialogues.title: A family photo
dialogues.context: Lucas shows his friend Helena a photo of his family.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Helena, esta é a minha família.
lines.en: Helena, this is my family.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: Que legal! Quem é este?
lines.en: How nice! Who is this?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Este é o meu pai e esta é a minha mãe.
lines.en: This is my father and this is my mother.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: Seus pais são jovens!
lines.en: Your parents are young!

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Obrigado! Eles são de Salvador. Este é o meu irmão Tiago, e esta é a minha irmã Clara.
lines.en: Thanks! They are from Salvador. This is my brother Tiago, and this is my sister Clara.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: Seu irmão é muito alto! E a sua irmã é casada?
lines.en: Your brother is very tall! And is your sister married?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: É, sim. O marido dela é argentino.
lines.en: Yes, she is. Her husband is Argentinian.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: Que legal! Eles têm filhos?
lines.en: How nice! Do they have children?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Têm uma filha. Ela é minha sobrinha e tem cinco anos.
lines.en: They have a daughter. She is my niece and is five years old.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: E você? Você é casado?
lines.en: And you? Are you married?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Não, sou solteiro, mas tenho uma namorada.
lines.en: No, I am single, but I have a girlfriend.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: Que bom!
lines.en: How nice!

dialogues.title: Talking about pets
dialogues.context: Fernanda and Marcos chat during a break at work and talk about their pets.

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.pt: Marcos, você tem um animal de estimação?
lines.en: Marcos, do you have a pet?

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Tenho, sim! Eu tenho um cachorro e dois gatos.
lines.en: Yes, I do! I have a dog and two cats.

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.pt: Que legal! Como se chama o cachorro?
lines.en: How nice! What is the dog called?

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Ele se chama Totó. Os gatos são da minha mãe.
lines.en: He is called Totó. The cats are my mother's.

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.pt: E como eles se chamam?
lines.en: And what are they called?

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Eles se chamam Mel e Bolinha.
lines.en: They are called Mel and Bolinha.

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: E você? Você tem um cachorro?
lines.en: And you? Do you have a dog?

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.pt: Não, mas minha irmã tem um gato. O nome dele é Simba.
lines.en: No, but my sister has a cat. His name is Simba.

lines.speaker: Marcos
lines.pt: Simba? Que nome legal!
lines.en: Simba? What a cool name!

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.pt: É! O gato dela é muito engraçado.
lines.en: Yes! Her cat is very funny.

dialogues.title: Sunday lunch with the family
dialogues.context: Pedro is at his aunt Rosa's house for Sunday lunch. He introduces Juliana, the cousin of his friend Ana, to his aunt.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.pt: Pedro, quem é ela?
lines.en: Pedro, who is she?

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Esta é a Juliana, tia. Ela é a prima da Ana.
lines.en: This is Juliana, Aunt Rosa. She is Ana's cousin.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.pt: Muito prazer, Juliana! Eu sou a tia do Pedro.
lines.en: Nice to meet you, Juliana! I am Pedro's aunt.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.pt: Prazer! A senhora é a irmã da mãe dele?
lines.en: Nice to meet you! Are you his mother's sister?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.pt: Sou, sim. A mãe dele é a minha irmã.
lines.en: Yes, I am. His mother is my sister.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: E o meu tio Carlos é o marido da tia Rosa.
lines.en: And my uncle Carlos is Aunt Rosa's husband.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.pt: A senhora tem filhos, dona Rosa?
lines.en: Do you have children, Dona Rosa?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.pt: Tenho dois filhos e uma filha. Os meus filhos são casados.
lines.en: I have two sons and a daughter. My children are married.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.pt: E netos?
lines.en: And grandchildren?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.pt: Tenho três netos lindos!
lines.en: I have three lovely grandchildren!

grammar.title: Articles and noun gender
grammar.explanation:
Every Portuguese noun is either masculine or feminine, and the article agrees with it. The definite article, the, is o for a masculine singular noun, a for a feminine singular noun, os for a masculine plural and as for a feminine plural. The indefinite article, a or an, is um, uma, and in the plural uns, umas, which mean some.

Most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -a are feminine: o filho, a filha; o tio, a tia. Learn the common exceptions: o dia, o mapa and many words in -ma such as o problema and o sistema are masculine, while a mão is feminine. Nouns ending in -ção, -são, -dade and -gem are normally feminine: a canção, a cidade, a viagem. Nouns ending in -e can be either, so learn them with the article: o leite, a noite, o nome, a tarde.

For people, the gender follows the person. Family words often come in pairs: o pai, a mãe; o irmão, a irmã; o avô, a avó. Nouns ending in -or usually add -a for women: o professor, a professora. Some nouns have one form for both, and the article shows the gender: o parente, a parente.

In Brazil the definite article is used before first names in everyday speech: a Ana, o Pedro. This sounds natural and is not rude. It is dropped when you address the person directly. Articles are also used in general statements where English has none: O café é bom, A família é importante.

examples.pt: O pai da Ana é médico.
A mãe do Pedro é professora.
Eu tenho um irmão e uma irmã.
examples.en: I have a brother and a sister.

examples.pt: Os meus avós são de Recife.

grammar.title: Regular plurals
grammar.explanation:
To make a noun plural, add -s if it ends in a vowel: casa, casas; filho, filhos; tia, tias. The article and the adjective also become plural: os filhos altos, as tias simpáticas. When the group includes at least one male, use the masculine plural: os irmãos can be brothers or brothers and sisters, os pais means parents, os avós means grandparents, os filhos means children.

Nouns ending in -r or -z add -es: mulher, mulheres; flor, flores; luz, luzes. Nouns ending in -m change to -ns: homem, homens; item, itens. Nouns ending in -al, -el, -ol or -ul change -l to -is: animal, animais; papel, papéis; hotel, hotéis. The accent changes if it is needed to keep the stress in the same syllable. Nouns ending in -s with a stressed last syllable add -es: país, países. If the last syllable is not stressed, the noun stays the same: o ônibus, os ônibus.

Nouns ending in -ão have three possible plurals, and you must learn each word: most take -ões (limão, limões; avião, aviões; canção, canções), a few take -ães (pão, pães; cão, cães), and some take -ãos (irmão, irmãos; mão, mãos). Irmãos is the one you need now. The plural of avô is avôs (grandfathers), but os avós is the usual word for grandparents, and it is also the plural of avó (grandmothers).

examples.pt: Os pais dela são de Curitiba.

grammar.title: Possessives
grammar.explanation:
Possessives agree with the thing that is owned, not with the owner. Minha irmã uses minha because irmã is feminine, whether the speaker is a man or a woman. The forms for my are meu, minha, meus and minhas. The forms for your (speaking to você) are seu, sua, seus and suas. The forms for our are nosso, nossa, nossos and nossas. In Brazil the article before a possessive is optional and usually left out in speech: meu pai and o meu pai are both normal.

Seu and sua can mean your, his, her or their, so they can be ambiguous. To be clear, Brazilians often use dele, dela, deles and delas, which come after the noun and agree with the owner: a casa dele (his house), a casa dela (her house), a casa deles (their house, masculine or mixed group), a casa delas (their house, all female). For a group that you address, de vocês is also used: a casa de vocês. Dele and dela do not change for the thing owned: os carros dele and a irmã dele.

The forms teu and tua exist for tu and are used in some regions and in writing, but you can skip them for now. A gente uses nosso and nossa as nós does: a gente tem nossa casa.

The question Qual é o seu nome? uses seu, and the answer Meu nome é Ana uses meu. These two phrases are among the most common uses of possessives in everyday speech.

grammar.title: Possession with de, ter, and marital status
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese has no apostrophe s. To say that something belongs to someone, use de plus the owner: o carro da Ana means Ana's car, literally the car of Ana. Because names take an article in Brazilian speech, de joins with it: de + a = da, de + o = do, de + as = das, de + os = dos. So you say a casa dos meus pais for my parents' house and o gato do Pedro for Pedro's cat. Without an article, de stays separate: o carro de Ana is also correct and more formal.

The same contraction happens with dele and dela: de + ele = dele, de + ela = dela, de + eles = deles, de + elas = delas. This explains why these words mean his and her: they literally say of him and of her.

Ter, which you learned in unit 4, is the main verb for having people and pets: Eu tenho dois irmãos, Ela tem um cachorro, Nós não temos filhos.

For marital status, use ser with an adjective that agrees with the person: Eu sou solteiro (a man), Ela é casada. People in a dating relationship say Tenho namorado or Tenho namorada. To ask for the name of a pet or person use Como se chama? and answer with se chama: O cachorro se chama Totó. The literal meaning is calls himself.

examples.pt: O carro da Ana é novo.
O cachorro é do meu irmão.
A casa dos meus avós é linda.
Eu tenho dois irmãos e uma irmã.
examples.en: I have two brothers and a sister.

examples.pt: Ela é casada e ele é solteiro.
examples.en: She is married and he is single.

culture.title: Family life in Brazil
culture.text:
Family is at the center of Brazilian social life. Sunday lunch with parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins is a weekly tradition for many families, and birthdays, baptisms and weddings are big events. Extended family is often close by, and it is common for adult children to live with their parents until they marry.

The words tio and tia are used very widely. Children call their parents' friends and their teachers tio and tia as a sign of affection, and a friend of the family can become tio Carlos or tia Rosa. Grandparents are often called vovô and vovó by small children, and vô and vó by adults. Godparents, padrinho and madrinha, are an important part of the family too, and a child's parents and godparents call each other compadre and comadre, words also used between very close friends.

Pets are increasingly part of the family. Dogs and cats are called animais de estimação, and many Brazilians treat them as members of the household. When people ask Você tem filhos? the answer may well be Tenho dois filhos e um cachorro. Family words are also used as terms of endearment. Strangers may address an older woman as tia or dona, and a street vendor may call a customer meu amigo or minha querida.
